what: Roberval balance with an added mass. This is Poise with one extra magenta 3L beam and two pins (1.5 g in the simulator’s part data) under the left pan; every other part and the program are unchanged. The two motors still move equal eccentric weights across level pans while the blue balance bars stay passive.
try: Open Poise Mass Control with its program, press Reset, then Run. Watch the blue bar as soon as the program starts: the heavier left side goes down and the balance swings.
Compare the five held pauses with the main Poise model. Here the bar is still swinging by up to several degrees, so a single pause does not show the settled weighing result.
Let the simulation keep running for about two minutes after the program finishes, then read the bar angle. It should settle near −2.9° (left side down).
why: The parallelogram keeps both pans level, so the extra mass acts as if it hung at the end of the 56 mm half-span, wherever on the pan it sits. Its weight produces a turning moment Δm·g·a. The orange ballast frame below the upper pivot produces a restoring moment that grows with the tilt angle, so the balance turns until the two moments are equal. Because the linkage has little damping, it overshoots and swings around that angle before settling.
matters: A control run shows that the main experiment’s level balance is not caused by a jammed or clamped linkage: the same mechanism responds clearly to 1.5 g. It also shows the difference between an instantaneous reading and a settled weighing result. In a headless run of the Brickwright simulator, each weight assembly’s centre of mass moved about 20 mm along the beam while the passive balance stayed within 0.046° of level (held means within 0.033° of each other); with the 1.5 g added-mass control it settled at −2.91° after 120 s, against a predicted −2.94°. These are simulation observations; no physical LEGO build has been tested.
question: The added mass is only 1.5 g. Will the balance tilt by a small fraction of a degree, by a few degrees, or all the way to its stops? And does it matter where on the left pan the mass sits?
answer: A few degrees: with a restoring stiffness of about 0.016 N·m/rad, θ ≈ −0.0015 kg × 9.81 m/s² × 0.056 m / 0.016 N·m/rad ≈ −0.051 rad ≈ −2.9°. In the ideal Roberval geometry its horizontal position on the pan does not matter. The first swing goes about twice as far, near −5.9°, before the motion decays.
further: Compare the late settled angle with the formula. Then estimate what mass would be needed to reach the fixed pan stops near ±17°, outside the qualified range.
Compare Parallel Lift, where a driven parallelogram carries a level tray but nothing weighs.
formula: Settled θ ≈ −Δm·g·a/κ; Δm = 1.5 g, a = 56 mm, κ ≈ 0.016 N·m/rad ⇒ θ ≈ −2.9°. Undamped first turning point ≈ 2θ ≈ −5.9°.
